I had this discussion a year ago when Filipino restaurants are starting to pop out in NYC. There's this one friend of mine who is so enamored with other culture and hates Filipino culture so much that I enjoyed a discussion because of different perspective.

My anti-pinoy friend pov why it will not be popular:

  1. There's no distinct filipino food. Everything was from other culture, from lumpia to pansit to adobo.
  2. Presentation is bad. We are not like thailand or china or malaysia where monarchy helped improved presentation of food.
  3. Filipino food do not have complex taste. It is basically, sweet, sour, sweet and salty. Unlike Italians with their herbs and Indian with their spices.

My POV

  1. Filipino food is comfort food. It's wasn't meant to serve to kings and queens but it was meant to be eaten with families and friends. (presentation wasn't important, it's more of the taste and who are you eating with)
  2. Every pinoy has their own 'better version' of the dish. Look at adobo, from the ingredients to the final output, its version is as many as our islands (e.g. adobo sa gata, adobong puti, adobong tuyo, twice cooked adobo, adobo with calamansi, adobo with pinya, etc.)
  3. Filipino food is so diverse and evolving. We are influenced by a lot of culture even before Magellan set foot in Visayas. And even until now, due to how receptive Filipinos in terms of food and the effect migrant pinoys/ofw, food from other cultures are starting to be part of our daily menu.

I think the way to market Filipino food shouldn't be the same with our Asian neighbors. I realized that nobody will truly enjoy Filipino Food just by tasting it. The Filipino part of our food is not only in the food itself but in how we prepare, serve and eat it. Eating for us is an event, a feast at least an experience. The way we buy the ingredients from palengke to preparing the food with relatives up to serving it to a big platter so every body can enjoy. We always eat when we want to interact with other people as if food is the key to a wonderful interaction. I always relate Filipino food with laughter, music, fun and never ending stories.

Up scaling our food with just presentation will not help a lot. We need to market it as something different in order to penetrate the world market. The authenticity of Filipino food is not on the food itself but on the experience on eating it. People should be reminded of home, of families, of their childhood get together, of all-night laughters and stories.

I think Jeepney in NYC is doing it already. They have boodle fest where they eat on a banana leaf. That is fun. But I'm not saying we should start forcing people to eat using their hands. I mean we should start introducing eating filipino food is an experience and at the center stage is our food.

It's been said before. Filipino food doesn't have identity. You may point to 'adobo' but in each region, there's a different concept to 'adobo.' Same goes to other dishes. There isn't a singular unifying distinctive dish to identify as Filipino.

If someone claims this is the real deal, other regions would say otherwise and at a Marketing standpoint, that's a problem.
There are some hidden gems in my area that can go up against mom's cooking. It's more home style cooking versus fine dining. All they really need is more word of mouth to spread the word.
